title: Images and AI
description: How AI tools work with images — generation, analysis, editing, and practical use cases.

data.text: AI is no longer text-only. Today's AI tools can see images, generate them, describe what's in them, and edit them. This lesson gives you a practical map of what each type of image AI can do — and when to use each one.

Image AI covers three fundamentally different capabilities that are often conflated. Generation creates a new image from a text description. Analysis (also called vision) understands and describes an image you provide. Editing modifies an existing image based on instructions. These use different underlying technologies, different tools, and different workflows — knowing which one you need is the first step to using image AI effectively.
The three types of image AI

data.text: How image generation works

Modern image generation models — DALL-E, Midjourney, Stable Diffusion, Flux — are trained on billions of image-text pairs scraped from the web. During training, they learn to associate visual patterns with language descriptions. At generation time, you provide a text prompt and the model synthesises pixels that match it, starting from random noise and refining it iteratively until a coherent image emerges. This process is called diffusion — the dominant technique behind most image generators today.

data.caption: Diffusion models start from noise and iteratively refine toward an image matching your prompt.
data.definition:
flowchart TD
  P[Text prompt] --> E[Text encoder]
  N[Random noise] --> D1[Denoising step 1]
  E --> D1
  D1 --> D2[Denoising step 2]
  D2 --> D3[...denoising steps]
  D3 --> IMG[Final image]

  style P fill:#ddf4ff,stroke:#0969da,color:#0550ae
  style IMG fill:#d1f3d8,stroke:#1a7f37,color:#1a7f37

data.text: One practical consequence of this process: image generators are probabilistic. The same prompt produces different results each time. There is no single 'correct' output for a given description — the model samples from a range of plausible images. This is why prompting for image generation is an iterative process: generate several variations, keep what works, refine what does not.
Image generation: create from text

cards.title: DALL-E 3 (OpenAI)
cards.description: Built directly into ChatGPT (paid tier). Best for quick, practical images: social media headers, presentation slides, mockups, and illustrations. Excellent at following detailed text descriptions precisely.
pros: Integrated in ChatGPT — no extra tool
Great at following complex text prompts

cards.title: Midjourney
cards.description: The gold standard for artistic and aesthetic quality. Best for beautiful, stylized, or mood-rich imagery. Used by designers and creative professionals. Requires a paid subscription and runs through Discord.

cards.title: Adobe Firefly
cards.description: Commercially safe image generation integrated into Adobe Creative Cloud. All training data was licensed — making it the safest choice for commercial use. Best for professional design workflows.

cards.title: Flux / Stable Diffusion (open)
cards.description: Open-source image models you can run locally or via third-party apps (Fal.ai, Replicate, RunDiffusion). Free and highly customizable but require more technical setup.
pros: Free or very cheap per image

data.text: Image analysis: understanding images you upload
All major AI chatbots now support "vision" — you can upload any image and ask questions about it. This is one of the most immediately useful and underused AI capabilities.

Vision models work differently from generation models. Rather than producing pixels, they encode the image into the same kind of vector representation used for text, allowing the language model to reason about both your words and the image content simultaneously. In practice, this means you can describe what you want to know about an image in plain language and get a coherent, contextual answer — as if you were describing the image to a knowledgeable colleague over the phone.

data.title: What AI can do with images you upload:
items: Describe and caption what is in a photo in natural language
Extract all text from screenshots, business cards, photos, and PDFs (OCR)
Analyze charts, graphs, and dashboards — describe trends and key numbers
Identify objects, products, logos, and scenes
Answer specific questions about the image ("How many items are on the shelf?")
Compare two images and describe their differences
Review a UI mockup or wireframe and give design feedback

data.title: Practical vision use cases
data.content:
1. Business card photo → "Extract all contact information as structured JSON"
2. Complex slide from a presentation → "Summarize the key message of this chart"
3. Screenshot of an error message → "What is causing this error and how do I fix it?"
4. Photo of a restaurant menu in another language → "Translate and describe the dishes"
5. Handwritten meeting notes → "Convert these notes to a typed summary"

data.title: Vision for data and documents
data.content:
Vision models are particularly powerful for extracting structure from images of documents and data:

- Photo of a whiteboard after a meeting → "List all action items and owners captured here"
- Screenshot of a complex Excel sheet → "Describe what this spreadsheet tracks and what the highlighted row means"
- Image of a paper form → "Convert this form into a JSON object with field names and values"
- Photo of a printed invoice → "Extract the line items, totals, and due date as a table"
- Screenshot of a web page → "What is the main call to action on this page and how prominent is it?"

This is especially useful when you have physical documents or screenshots you cannot copy text from directly.

data.text: Upload a screenshot of any complex chart to Claude or ChatGPT and ask "What are the 3 most important trends visible in this data?" It saves minutes of manual reading and often surfaces patterns you would miss.
What vision models get wrong
Vision models are impressive but not infallible. Knowing their common failure modes helps you verify the outputs that matter most.

rows: Models frequently miscount objects in dense or complex images
Ask the model to reason step-by-step; verify counts manually for critical use
Low-resolution or small text is often misread or missed
Crop and zoom in on the relevant section before uploading
Relative positions of objects ('left of', 'behind') can be unreliable
Describe the spatial relationship explicitly and ask the model to confirm
Subtle colour differences may be missed or misnamed
Use colour-picker tools for precise colour values
Messy or highly stylised handwriting degrades accuracy significantly
Photograph under good lighting; confirm critical words

data.text: Image editing: modifying existing images with AI

AI image editing goes beyond filters. Modern tools can remove objects and fill the space realistically, change backgrounds, extend an image beyond its original borders (outpainting), add new elements into a scene, or change the style of an entire image. The technical capability underneath most of these features is inpainting — the same diffusion process used for generation, applied to a masked region of an existing image rather than a blank canvas.

rows: Remove an object and fill the background, or replace it with something else
Adobe Firefly, DALL-E in ChatGPT, Photoshop AI
Extend the image beyond its original borders
Replace the background while keeping the subject
Adobe Firefly, Canva AI, Remove.bg + AI
Apply a visual style to an existing image
Increase resolution and add detail to low-res images
Topaz Gigapixel, Magnific AI, SDXL upscalers

data.text: Writing effective image generation prompts

Effective image prompts are more structured than text prompts. Where text generation benefits from conversational context, image generation benefits from layered specificity: what is in the scene, how it looks, how it is lit, and what mood it conveys. The prompt elements below are the standard vocabulary — you do not need all of them every time, but the more you include, the more control you have over the output.

rows: "A woman working at a standing desk"

data.title: Weak prompt vs. strong prompt
data.content:
Weak: "A person at a desk"
Strong: "A young woman with short dark hair working at a minimalist standing desk, soft natural light from a window to the left, calm and focused mood, shallow depth of field, photorealistic, 16:9 aspect ratio"

Both prompts produce an image. The strong prompt produces an image that matches a specific vision. The difference is not creativity — it is specificity. Think of yourself as an art director briefing a photographer: the more clearly you describe what you want, the closer the output will be to what you imagined.

If you are unsure how to describe a style you have in mind, ask a language model first: "How would I describe the visual style of [reference] for an image generation prompt?" This converts vague aesthetic intuitions into concrete prompt vocabulary.

data.text: Copyright, commercial use, and common pitfalls
AI-generated images sit in evolving legal territory. The main considerations for practical use are training data licensing, output ownership, and what you can and cannot generate.

Training data and commercial safety: most image generators were trained on data scraped from the web without explicit licensing from the original creators. Adobe Firefly is the notable exception — its training data was licensed, making it the safest choice for commercial work. For DALL-E, Midjourney, and open-source models, commercial use terms vary by platform and continue to evolve. Check each platform's current terms of service before using generated images in commercial contexts.

Style prompting: asking a model to generate an image 'in the style of [living artist]' is legal in most jurisdictions but ethically contested and increasingly restricted by the platforms themselves. Most tools will generate in the style of a movement or period (impressionist, bauhaus, Art Deco) without issue, but may decline to produce close imitations of specific named living artists.

Common generation artifacts to watch for: AI-generated images frequently contain specific tell-tale errors — extra or malformed fingers and hands, garbled or nonsensical text embedded in the image, symmetry errors in faces, inconsistent lighting across a scene, and merged objects at scene edges. Always inspect generated images carefully before using them, especially for anything client-facing or public.

data.title: Text in generated images is almost always wrong
data.text: Image generators cannot reliably render legible text. Signs, labels, logos, and captions in generated images almost always contain garbled characters. If you need text in an image, generate the image without text and add the text in a design tool like Canva or Photoshop afterwards.

data.title: Image AI quick reference
points: Generation: DALL-E (quick + integrated), Midjourney (highest quality), Firefly (commercial safe)
Analysis (vision): ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini all support it — upload and ask questions
OCR: AI reliably reads text from photos, screenshots, and even messy handwriting
Editing: Adobe Firefly, Canva AI, and DALL-E in-painting for modifying existing images
Always check generated images for artifacts — extra fingers, garbled text, merged faces
Strong prompts layer subject + style + lighting + mood + composition
Ask a language model to help convert your style intuitions into prompt vocabulary
For commercial use, Adobe Firefly is the safest option — training data was licensed
Vision models count and spatially reason poorly — verify critical details manually
